cheat.1.md
# cheat

`cheat` allows you to create and view interactive cheatsheets on the
command-line. It was designed to help remind *nix system administrators of
options for commands that they use frequently, but not frequently enough to
remember.

## Example
The next time you're forced to disarm a nuclear weapon without consulting
Google, you may run:

```sh
cheat tar
```

You will be presented with a cheatsheet resembling the following:

```sh
# To extract an uncompressed archive:
tar -xvf '/path/to/foo.tar'

# To extract a .gz archive:
tar -xzvf '/path/to/foo.tgz'

# To create a .gz archive:
tar -czvf '/path/to/foo.tgz' '/path/to/foo/'

# To extract a .bz2 archive:
tar -xjvf '/path/to/foo.tgz'

# To create a .bz2 archive:
tar -cjvf '/path/to/foo.tgz' '/path/to/foo/'
```

## Installing
See [INSTALLING.md][] for installation and configuration instructions.

## Usage
To view a cheatsheet:

```sh
cheat tar      # a "top-level" cheatsheet
cheat foo/bar  # a "nested" cheatsheet
```

To edit a cheatsheet:

```sh
cheat -e tar     # opens the "tar" cheatsheet for editing, or creates it if it does not exist
cheat -e foo/bar # nested cheatsheets are accessed like this
```

To view the configured cheatpaths:

```sh
cheat -d
```

To list all available cheatsheets:

```sh
cheat -l
```

To briefly list all cheatsheets (names and tags only):

```sh
cheat -b
```

To list all cheatsheets that are tagged with "networking":

```sh
cheat -l -t networking
```

To list all cheatsheets on the "personal" path:

```sh
cheat -l -p personal
```

To search for the phrase "ssh" among cheatsheets:

```sh
cheat -s ssh
```

To search (by regex) for cheatsheets that contain an IP address:

```sh
cheat -r -s '(?:[0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}'
```

Flags may be combined in intuitive ways. Example: to search sheets on the
"personal" cheatpath that are tagged with "networking" and match a regex:

```sh
cheat -p personal -t networking --regex -s '(?:[0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}'
```

## Cheatsheets
Cheatsheets are plain-text files with no file extension, and are named
according to the command used to view them:

```sh
cheat tar     # file is named "tar"
cheat foo/bar # file is named "bar", in a "foo" subdirectory
```

Cheatsheet text may optionally be preceded by a YAML frontmatter header that
assigns tags and specifies syntax:

```
---
syntax: javascript
tags: [ array, map ]
---
// To map over an array:
const squares = [1, 2, 3, 4].map(x => x * x);
```

## Cheatpaths
Cheatsheets are stored on "cheatpaths", which are directories that contain
cheatsheets. Cheatpaths are specified in the `conf.yml` file.

It can be useful to configure `cheat` against multiple cheatpaths. A common
pattern is to store cheatsheets from multiple repositories on individual
cheatpaths:

```yaml
# conf.yml:
# ...
cheatpaths:
  - name: community                   # a name for the cheatpath
    path: ~/documents/cheat/community # the path's location on the filesystem
    tags: [ community ]               # these tags will be applied to all sheets on the path
    readonly: true                    # if true, `cheat` will not create new cheatsheets here

  - name: personal
    path: ~/documents/cheat/personal  # this is a separate directory and repository than above
    tags: [ personal ]
    readonly: false                   # new sheets may be written here
# ...
```

The `readonly` option instructs `cheat` not to edit (or create) any cheatsheets
on the path. This is useful to prevent merge-conflicts from arising on upstream
cheatsheet repositories.

If a user attempts to edit a cheatsheet on a read-only cheatpath, `cheat` will
transparently copy that sheet to a writeable directory before opening it for
editing.

### Directory-scoped Cheatpaths
At times, it can be useful to closely associate cheatsheets with a directory on
your filesystem. `cheat` facilitates this by searching for a `.cheat` directory
in the current working directory and its ancestors (similar to how `git` locates
`.git` directories). The nearest `.cheat` directory found will (temporarily) be
added to the cheatpaths. This means you can place a `.cheat` directory at your
project root and it will be available from any subdirectory within that project.

## Autocompletion
`cheat` can generate shell completion scripts for `bash`, `zsh`, `fish`, and
`powershell` via the `--completion` flag:

```sh
cheat --completion bash
cheat --completion zsh
cheat --completion f
```

```sh

cheat --completion fish
cheat --completion powershell
```

Pipe the output to the appropriate location for your shell. For example:

```sh
# bash (user-local)
mkdir -p ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions
cheat --completion bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/cheat

# bash (system-wide)
cheat --completion bash > /etc/bash_completion.d/cheat

# zsh (ensure the directory is on your fpath)
cheat --completion zsh > "${fpath[1]}/_cheat"

# fish
cheat --completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/cheat.fish
```

Completions are dynamically generated and include cheatsheet names, tags, and
cheatpath names.

# cheat

`cheat` allows you to create and view interactive cheatsheets on the
command-line. It was designed to help remind *nix system administrators of
options for commands that they use frequently, but not frequently enough to
remember.

## Example
The next time you're forced to disarm a nuclear weapon without consulting
Google, you may run:

```sh
cheat tar
```

You will be presented with a cheatsheet resembling the following:

```sh
# To extract an uncompressed archive:
tar -xvf '/path/to/foo.tar'

# To extract a .gz archive:
tar -xzvf '/path/to/foo.tgz'

# To create a .gz archive:
tar -czvf '/path/to/foo.tgz' '/path/to/foo/'

# To extract a .bz2 archive:
tar -xjvf '/path/to/foo.tgz'

# To create a .bz2 archive:
tar -cjvf '/path/to/foo.tgz' '/path/to/foo/'
```

## Installing
See [INSTALLING.md][] for installation and configuration instructions.

## Usage
To view a cheatsheet:

```sh
cheat tar      # a "top-level" cheatsheet
cheat foo/bar  # a "nested" cheatsheet
```

To edit a cheatsheet:

```sh
cheat -e tar     # opens the "tar" cheatsheet for editing, or creates it if it does not exist
cheat -e foo/bar # nested cheatsheets are accessed like this
```

To view the configured cheatpaths:

```sh
cheat -d
```

To list all available cheatsheets:

```sh
cheat -l
```

To briefly list all cheatsheets (names and tags only):

```sh
cheat -b
```

To list all cheatsheets that are tagged with "networking":

```sh
cheat -l -t networking
```

To list all cheatsheets on the "personal" path:

```sh
cheat -l -p personal
```

To search for the phrase "ssh" among cheatsheets:

```sh
cheat -s ssh
```

To search (by regex) for cheatsheets that contain an IP address:

```sh
cheat -r -s '(?:[0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}'
```

Flags may be combined in intuitive ways. Example: to search sheets on the
"personal" cheatpath that are tagged with "networking" and match a regex:

```sh
cheat -p personal -t networking --regex -s '(?:[0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}'
```

## Cheatsheets
Cheatsheets are plain-text files with no file extension, and are named
according to the command used to view them:

```sh
cheat tar     # file is named "tar"
cheat foo/bar # file is named "bar", in a "foo" subdirectory
```

Cheatsheet text may optionally be preceded by a YAML frontmatter header that
assigns tags and specifies syntax:

```
---
syntax: javascript
tags: [ array, map ]
---
// To map over an array:
const squares = [1, 2, 3, 4].map(x => x * x);
```

## Cheatpaths
Cheatsheets are stored on "cheatpaths", which are directories that contain
cheatsheets. Cheatpaths are specified in the `conf.yml` file.

It can be useful to configure `cheat` against multiple cheatpaths. A common
pattern is to store cheatsheets from multiple repositories on individual
cheatpaths:

```yaml
# conf.yml:
# ...
cheatpaths:
  - name: community                   # a name for the cheatpath
    path: ~/documents/cheat/community # the path's location on the filesystem
    tags: [ community ]               # these tags will be applied to all sheets on the path
    readonly: true                    # if true, `cheat` will not create new cheatsheets here

  - name: personal
    path: ~/documents/cheat/personal  # this is a separate directory and repository than above
    tags: [ personal ]
    readonly: false                   # new sheets may be written here
# ...
```

The `readonly` option instructs `cheat` not to edit (or create) any cheatsheets
on the path. This is useful to prevent merge-conflicts from arising on upstream
cheatsheet repositories.

If a user attempts to edit a cheatsheet on a read-only cheatpath, `cheat` will
transparently copy that sheet to a writeable directory before opening it for
editing.

### Directory-scoped Cheatpaths
At times, it can be useful to closely associate cheatsheets with a directory on
your filesystem. `cheat` facilitates this by searching for a `.cheat` directory
in the current working directory and its ancestors (similar to how `git` locates
`.git` directories). The nearest `.cheat` directory found will (temporarily) be
added to the cheatpaths. This means you can place a `.cheat` directory at your
project root and it will be available from any subdirectory within that project.

## Autocompletion
`cheat` can generate shell completion scripts for `bash`, `zsh`, `fish`, and
`powershell` via the `--completion` flag:

```sh
cheat --completion bash
cheat --completion zsh
cheat --completion fish
cheat --completion powershell
```

Pipe the output to the appropriate location for your shell. For example:

```sh
# bash (user-local)
mkdir -p ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions
cheat --completion bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/cheat

# bash (system-wide)
cheat --completion bash > /etc/bash_completion.d/cheat

# zsh (ensure the directory is on your fpath)
cheat --completion zsh > "${fpath[1]}/_cheat"

# fish
cheat --completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/cheat.fish
```

Completions are dynamically generated and include cheatshee

% CHEAT(1) | General Commands Manual

NAME
====

**cheat** — create and view command-line cheatsheets

SYNOPSIS
========

| **cheat** \[options] \[_CHEATSHEET_]

DESCRIPTION
===========
**cheat** allows you to create and view interactive cheatsheets on the
command-line. It was designed to help remind \*nix system administrators of
options for commands that they use frequently, but not frequently enough to
remember.

OPTIONS
=======

--init
: Print a config file to stdout.

--conf
: Display the config file path.

-a, --all
: Search among all cheatpaths.

-b, --brief
: List cheatsheets without file paths.

-c, --colorize
: Colorize output.

-d, --directories
: List cheatsheet directories.

-e, --edit=_CHEATSHEET_
: Open _CHEATSHEET_ for editing.

-l, --list
: List available cheatsheets.

-p, --path=_PATH_
: Filter only to sheets found on path _PATH_.

-r, --regex
: Treat search _PHRASE_ as a regular expression.

-s, --search=_PHRASE_
: Search cheatsheets for _PHRASE_.

-t, --tag=_TAG_
: Filter only to sheets tagged with _TAG_.

-T, --tags
: List all tags in use.

-u, --update
: Update git-backed cheatpaths by pulling the latest changes.

-v, --version
: Print the version number.

--rm=_CHEATSHEET_
: Remove (deletes) _CHEATSHEET_.

--completion=_SHELL_
: Generate a shell completion script. _SHELL_ must be one of: **bash**,
**zsh**, **fish**, **powershell**.


EXAMPLES
========

To view the foo cheatsheet:
: cheat _foo_

To edit (or create) the foo cheatsheet:
: cheat -e _foo_

To edit (or create) the foo/bar cheatsheet on the 'work' cheatpath:
: cheat -p _work_ -e _foo/bar_

To view all cheatsheet directories:
: cheat -d

To list all available cheatsheets:
: cheat -l

To briefly list all cheatsheets whose titles match 'apt':
: cheat -b _apt_

To list all tags in use:
: cheat -T

To list available cheatsheets that are tagged as 'personal':
: cheat -l -t _personal_

To search for 'ssh' among all cheatsheets, and colorize matches:
: cheat -c -s _ssh_

To search (by regex) for cheatsheets that contain an IP address:
: cheat -c -r -s _'(?:[0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}'_

To remove (delete) the foo/bar cheatsheet:
: cheat --rm _foo/bar_

To update all git-backed cheatpaths:
: cheat --update

To update only the 'community' cheatpath:
: cheat -u -p _community_

To view the configuration file path:
: cheat --conf


FILES
=====

Configuration
-------------
**cheat** is configured via a YAML file that is conventionally named
_conf.yml_.  **cheat** will search for _conf.yml_ in varying locations,
depending upon your platform:

### Linux, OSX, and other Unixes ###

1. **CHEAT_CONFIG_PATH**
2. **XDG_CONFIG_HOME**/cheat/conf.yml
3. **$HOME**/.config/cheat/conf.yml
4. **$HOME**/.cheat/conf.yml
5. /etc/cheat/conf.yml

### Windows ###

1. **CHEAT_CONFIG_PATH**
2. **APPDATA**/cheat/conf.yml
3. **PROGRAMDATA**/cheat/conf.yml

**cheat** will search in the order specified above. The first _conf.yml_
encountered will be respected.

If **cheat** cannot locate a config file, it will ask if you'd like to generate
one automatically. Alternatively, you may also generate a config file manually
by running **cheat --init** and saving its output to the appropriate location
for your platform.


Cheatpaths
----------
**cheat** reads its cheatsheets from "cheatpaths", which are the directories in
which cheatsheets are stored. Cheatpaths may be configured in _conf.yml_, and
viewed via **cheat -d**.

For detailed instructions on how to configure cheatpaths, please refer to the
comments in conf.yml.


Autocompletion
--------------
**cheat** can generate shell completion scripts for **bash**, **zsh**,
**fish**, and **powershell** via the **--completion** flag:

    cheat --completion bash
    cheat --completion zsh
    cheat --completion fish
    cheat --completion powershell

Completions are dynamically generated and include cheatsheet names, tags, and
cheatpath names.

To install completions, pipe the output to the appropriate location for your
shell. For example, on **bash**:

    cheat --completion bash > /etc/bash_completion.d/cheat

Or for the current user only:

    cheat --completion bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/cheat

For **zsh**, you may need to add the completions directory to your **fpath**:

    cheat --completion zsh > "${fpath[1]}/_cheat"

For **fish**:

    cheat --completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/cheat.fish


ENVIRONMENT
===========

**CHEAT_CONFIG_PATH**

: The path at which the config file is available. If **CHEAT_CONFIG_PATH** is
set, all other config paths will be ignored.

RETURN VALUES
=============

0. Successful termination

1. Application error

2. Cheatsheet(s) not found


BUGS
====

See GitHub issues: <https://github.com/cheat/cheat/issues>

======

Christopher Allen Lane <chris@chris-allen-lane.com>

========

# Installing
`cheat` has no runtime dependencies. As such, installing it is generally
straightforward. There are a few methods available:

## Install manually
### Unix-like
On Unix-like systems, you may simply paste the following snippet into your terminal:

```sh
cd /tmp \
  && wget https://github.com/cheat/cheat/releases/download/5.0.0/cheat-linux-amd64.gz \
  && gunzip cheat-linux-amd64.gz \
  && chmod +x cheat-linux-amd64 \
  && sudo mv cheat-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/cheat
```

You may need to need to change the version number (`5.0.0`) and the archive
(`cheat-linux-amd64.gz`) depending on your platform.

See the [releases page][releases] for a list of supported platforms.

### Windows
On Windows, download the appropriate binary from the [releases page][releases],
unzip the archive, and place the `cheat.exe` executable on your `PATH`.

## Install via `go install`
If you have `go` version `>=1.26` available on your `PATH`, you can install
`cheat` via `go install`:

```sh
go install github.com/cheat/cheat/cmd/cheat@latest
```

## Install via package manager
Several community-maintained packages are also available:

Package manager  | Package(s)
---------------- | -----------
aur              | [cheat][pkg-aur-cheat], [cheat-bin][pkg-aur-cheat-bin]
brew             | [cheat][pkg-brew]
docker           | [docker-cheat][pkg-docker]
nix              | [nixos.cheat][pkg-nix]
snap             | [cheat][pkg-snap]

## Configuring
Three things must be done before you can use `cheat`:
1. A config file must be generated
2. [`cheatpaths`][cheatpaths] must be configured
3. [Community cheatsheets][community] must be downloaded

On first run, `cheat` will run an installer that will do all of the above
automatically. After the installer is complete, it is strongly advised that you
view the configuration file that was generated, as you may want to change some
of its default values (to enable colorization, change the paginator, etc).

### conf.yml
`cheat` is configured by a YAML file that will be auto-generated on first run.

By default, the config file is assumed to exist on an XDG-compliant
configuration path like `~/.config/cheat/conf.yml`. If you would like to store
it elsewhere, you may export a `CHEAT_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable that
specifies its path:

```sh
export CHEAT_CONFIG_PATH="~/.dotfiles/cheat/conf.yml"
```

            printf "\n"
            printf "%s\n" "${activeHelp[@]}"

            if ((${#COMPREPLY[*]} == 0)); then
                # When there are no completion choices from the program, file completion
                # may kick in if the program has not disabled it; in such a case, we want
                # to know if any files will match what the user typed, so that we know if
                # there will be completions presented, so that we know how to handle ActiveHelp.
                # To find out, we actually trigger the file completion ourselves;
                # the call to _filedir will fill COMPREPLY if files match.
                if (((directive & shellCompDirectiveNoFileComp) == 0)); then
                    __cheat_debug "Listing files"
                    _filedir
                fi
            fi

            if ((${#COMPREPLY[*]} != 0)); then
                # If there are completion choices to be shown, print a delimiter.
                # Re-printing the command-line will automatically be done
                # by the shell when it prints the completion choices.
                printf -- "--"
            else
                # When there are no completion choices at all, we need
                # to re-print the command-line since the shell will
                # not be doing it itself.
                __cheat_reprint_commandLine
            fi
        elif [ $COMP_TYPE -eq 37 ] || [ $COMP_TYPE -eq 42 ]; then
            # For completion type: menu-complete/menu-complete-backward and insert-completions
            # the completions are immediately inserted into the command-line, so we first
            # print the activeHelp message and reprint the command-line since the shell won't.
            printf "\n"
            printf "%s\n" "${activeHelp[@]}"

            __cheat_reprint_commandLine
        fi
    fi
}

__cheat_reprint_commandLine() {
    # The prompt format is only available from bash 4.4.
    # We test if it is available before using it.
    if (x=${PS1@P}) 2> /dev/null; then
        printf "%s" "${PS1@P}${COMP_LINE[@]}"
    else
        # Can't print the prompt.  Just print the
        # text the user had typed, it is workable enough.
        printf "%s" "${COMP_LINE[@]}"
    fi
}

import subprocess, os, shutil, pathlib, textwrap, sys
HOME="/tmp/th"
EXE="/workspace/executable"
def setup(conf=None):
    shutil.rmtree(HOME, ignore_errors=True)
    os.makedirs(f"{HOME}/personal/sub", exist_ok=True)
    os.makedirs(f"{HOME}/work", exist_ok=True)
    os.makedirs(f"{HOME}/community", exist_ok=True)
    os.makedirs(f"{HOME}/.config/cheat", exist_ok=True)
    if conf is None:
        conf = f"""---
editor: /bin/true
colorize: false
style: monokai
formatter: terminal256
pager: cat
cheatpaths:
  - name: personal
    path: {HOME}/personal
    tags: [ personal ]
    readonly: false
  - name: work
    path: {HOME}/work
    tags: [ work ]
    readonly: false
  - name: community
    path: {HOME}/community
    tags: [ community ]
    readonly: true
"""
    open(f"{HOME}/.config/cheat/conf.yml","w").write(conf)
    # sheets
    open(f"{HOME}/personal/tar","w").write("# personal tar\ntar -xvf foo\n")
    open(f"{HOME}/community/tar","w").write("# community tar\ntar -czvf bar\nssh info\n")
    open(f"{HOME}/work/ssh","w").write("---\nsyntax: bash\ntags: [ networking, ssh ]\n---\n# ssh sheet\nssh user@host\nIP 10.0.0.1\n")

    open(f"{HOME}/personal/alpha","w").write("alpha sheet ssh\n")
    open(f"{HOME}/work/beta","w").write("---\ntags: [ networking ]\n---\nbeta content\n")

def run(args, env_extra=None, input_data=None, cwd=None):
    env=dict(os.environ); env["HOME"]=HOME
    env.pop("CHEAT_CONFIG_PATH",None); env.pop("XDG_CONFIG_HOME",None)
    env.pop("VISUAL",None); env.pop("EDITOR",None); env.pop("PAGER",None)
    if env_extra: env.update(env_extra)
    r=subprocess.run([EXE]+args, input=input_data, capture_output=True, text=True, env=env, cwd=cwd or "/tmp")

    if r.stdout: print("OUT:", repr(r.stdout))
    if r.stderr: print("ERR:", repr(r.stderr))
    print("---")
    return r

if __name__=="__main__":

import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'/tmp')
from probe import setup, run, HOME
import os
def write_editor(path, body):
    open(path,"w").write(body); os.chmod(path,0o755)
def scenario(label, editor_conf, args, env=None, editor_files=None, sheets_extra=None, cheatpath_conf=None):
    setup()
    # editors scripts
    if editor_files:
        for fn,body in editor_files.items():
            write_editor(f"{HOME}/{fn}", body.replace("HOME_DIR",HOME))
    if sheets_extra:
        for rel,content in sheets_extra.items():
            p=os.path.join(HOME,rel); os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(p),exist_ok=True); open(p,"w").write(content)
    if cheatpath_conf is None:
        cheatpath_conf=f"""cheatpaths:
  - name: personal
    path: {HOME}/personal
    tags: [personal]
    readonly: false
  - name: work
    path: {HOME}/work
    tags: [work]
    readonly: false
  - name: community
    path: {HOME}/community
    tags: [community]
    readonly: true
"""
    open(f"{HOME}/.config/cheat/conf.yml","w").write(f"editor: {editor_conf}\npager: cat\n"+cheatpath_conf)
    print("SCENARIO",label)
    r=run(args, env_extra=env)
    print("log:", repr(open(f"{HOME}/editor.log").read()) if os.path.exists(f"{HOME}/editor.log") else None)
    # list relevant new files
    for base in ["personal","work","community"]:
        for root,dirs,files in os.walk(f"{HOME}/{base}"):
            dirs.sort(); files.sort()
            for f in files:
                fp=os.path.join(root,f); print(" file",fp,repr(open(fp).read()))
    print("==")

good="#!/bin/sh\nprintf 'GOOD:%s\\n' \"$*\" >> HOME_DIR/editor.log\nfor last; do :; done\nprintf 'edited\\n' >> \"$last\"\n"
vis="#!/bin/sh\nprintf 'VISUAL:%s\\n' \"$*\" >> HOME_DIR/editor.log\nfor last; do :; done\nprintf 'visualedit\\n' >> \"$last\"\n"
env_ed="#!/bin/sh\nprintf 'ENVED:%s\\n' \"$*\" >> HOME_DIR/editor.log\nfor last; do :; done\nprintf 'envedit\\n' >> \"$last\"\n"
fail="#!/bin/sh\necho editor-stdout-msg\necho editor-stderr-msg >&2\nexit 3\n"
scenario("editor env overrides config", f"{HOME}/good", ["-e","alpha"], env={"EDITOR":f"{HOME}/enved"}, editor_files={"good":good,"enved":env_ed})
scenario("VISUAL overrides EDITOR and config", f"{HOME}/good", ["-e","alpha"], env={"EDITOR":f"{HOME}/enved","VISUAL":f"{HOME}/vis"}, editor_files={"good":good,"enved":env_ed,"vis":vis})
scenario("VISUAL empty, EDITOR used", f"{HOME}/good", ["-e","alpha"], env={"EDITOR":f"{HOME}/enved","VISUAL":""}, editor_files={"good":good,"enved":env_ed,"vis":vis})
scenario("editor with args", f"{HOME}/good --flag 'quoted arg' -x", ["-e","alpha"], editor_files={"good":good})
scenario("editor fails existing", f"{HOME}/fail", ["-e","alpha"], editor_files={"fail":fail})
scenario("editor fails new sheet", f"{HOME}/fail", ["-e","brandnew"], editor_files={"fail":fail})
scenario("editor nonexist", "/nope/editorZZZ", ["-e","alpha"])

import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'/tmp')
from probe import setup, run, HOME
import os, subprocess, shutil
def git(args,cwd):
    subprocess.run(["git"]+args,cwd=cwd,capture_output=True,text=True,env={**os.environ,"HOME":HOME,"GIT_AUTHOR_NAME":"a","GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL":"a@a","GIT_COMMITTER_NAME":"a","GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL":"a@a"})
def case(label, fn=None, args=["-u"]):
    setup()
    if fn: fn()
    print("CASE",label)
    run(args)

def mk_git_no_remote():
    git(["init","-q"],f"{HOME}/personal"); git(["add","."],f"{HOME}/personal"); git(["commit","-qm","init"],f"{HOME}/personal")
def mk_git_dotfile_only():
    os.makedirs(f"{HOME}/personal/.git",exist_ok=True)
def mk_git_file():
    open(f"{HOME}/personal/.git","w").write("gitdir: /elsewhere\n")
def mk_bare_remote_and_clone():
    # create remote bare from work? Simpler: init personal as repo commit, clone bare to HOME/remote.git, set origin, then make new commit in a separate clone and push? We'll do step in fn later
    git(["init","-q"],f"{HOME}/personal"); git(["add","."],f"{HOME}/personal"); git(["commit","-qm","init"],f"{HOME}/personal")
    subprocess.run(["git","clone","-q","--bare",f"{HOME}/personal",f"{HOME}/remote.git"],capture_output=True)
    git(["remote","add","origin",f"{HOME}/remote.git"],f"{HOME}/personal")
    # upstream branch config clone style: set branch upstream
    branch=subprocess.run(["git","branch","--show-current"],cwd=f"{HOME}/personal",capture_output=True,text=True).stdout.strip() or "master"
    git(["branch",f"--set-upstream-to=origin/{branch}",branch],f"{HOME}/personal")

case("no git")
case("git no remote", mk_git_no_remote)
case("dotgit empty dir", mk_git_dotfile_only)
case("dotgit file bogus", mk_git_file)
case("git with local bare remote up to date", mk_bare_remote_and_clone)
case("filter personal git", mk_git_no_remote, ["-u","-p","personal"])
case("filter work no git", mk_git_no_remote, ["-u","-p","work"])
case("update tag filter? ", mk_git_no_remote, ["-u","-t","personal"])

# Now test actual pull: advance remote
setup(); mk_bare_remote_and_clone()
# clone remote to other, add sheet, push
subprocess.run(["git","clone","-q",f"{HOME}/remote.git",f"{HOME}/other"],capture_output=True,env={**os.environ,"HOME":HOME})
open(f"{HOME}/other/newsheet","w").write("new from remote\n")
git(["add","."],f"{HOME}/other"); git(["commit","-qm","add"],f"{HOME}/other"); git(["push","-q","origin","HEAD"],f"{HOME}/other")
print("CASE advance remote, before update files personal", os.listdir(f"{HOME}/personal"))
run(["-u","-p","personal"])
print("after", os.listdir(f"{HOME}/personal"), open(f"{HOME}/personal/newsheet").read() if os.path.exists(f"{HOME}/personal/newsheet") else None)
# dirty working tree then advance remote again
open(f"{HOME}/personal/tar","w").write("dirty local\n")
open(f"{HOME}/other/tar","w").write("remote changed tar\n")
open(f"{HOME}/other/another","w").write("another\n")
git(["add","."],f"{HOME}/other"); git(["commit","-qm","change"],f"{HOME}/other"); git(["push","-q","origin","HEAD"],f"{HOME}/other")
print("CASE dirty conflicting pull")
run(["-u","-p","personal"])
print("personal tar", open(f"{HOME}/personal/tar").read(), "another exists", os.path.exists(f"{HOME}/personal/another"))

import os,pty,sys,subprocess,select,shutil
HOME="/tmp/dth"
sys.path.insert(0,'/tmp')
from diff2 import setup
def run_pty(exe,conf,args):
    setup(conf=conf)
    env=dict(os.environ); env["HOME"]=HOME
    for k in ["CHEAT_CONFIG_PATH","XDG_CONFIG_HOME","VISUAL","EDITOR"]: env.pop(k,None)
    pid,fd=pty.fork()
    if pid==0:
        os.chdir("/tmp"); os.execve(exe,[exe]+args,env)
    out=b""
    while True:
        try:
            r,_,_=select.select([fd],[],[],2)
            if not r: break
            d=os.read(fd,4096)
            if not d: break
            out+=d
        except OSError: break
    _,st=os.waitpid(pid,0)

// ---------- update (git) ----------

func doUpdate(cfg *Config, opts *options, pathFiltered []Cheatpath) error {
	failed := false
	for _, cp := range pathFiltered {
		status, isErr := updateCheatpath(cp.Path)
		line := fmt.Sprintf("%s: %s\n", cp.Name, status)
		if isErr {
			fmt.Fprint(os.Stderr, line)
			failed = true
		} else {

	}
	if failed {
		return errExitSilent(1)

	return nil
}

func gitCmd(dir string, args ...string) (string, error) {
	cmd := exec.Command("git", append([]string{"-c", "safe.directory=*", "-C", dir}, args...)...)
	out, err := cmd.CombinedOutput()
	return strings.TrimSpace(string(out)), err
}

func updateCheatpath(path string) (string, bool) {
	// Determine git repo: .git must exist (dir or file) and git rev-parse works with GIT_DIR discovery only at this dir.
	// Use `git -C path rev-parse --git-dir`; but this would find parent repos. The original go-git PlainOpen only opens repo at exact path.
	// So first require path/.git exists.
	gitPath := filepath.Join(path, ".git")
	if _, err := os.Stat(gitPath); err != nil {
		return "skipped (not a git repository)", false
	}
	// validate repo at this path
	if _, err := gitCmd(path, "rev-parse", "--git-dir"); err != nil {
		return "skipped (not a git repository)", false
	}
	if fi, err := os.Lstat(gitPath); err == nil && fi.Mode().IsRegular() {
		return "error (object not found)", true
	}
	// check git-dir resolves to this .git (roughly) to avoid parent repo case when .git is bogus file etc handled above by rev-parse error
	// dirty?
	out, err := gitCmd(path, "status", "--porcelain", "--untracked-files=all")
	if err == nil && out != "" {
		return "skipped (dirty worktree)", false
	}
	// remote origin?
	remoteURL, err := gitCmd(path, "remote", "get-url", "origin")
	if err != nil {
		return "error (remote not found)", true
	}
	if strings.HasPrefix(remoteURL, "http://") || strings.HasPrefix(remoteURL, "https://") {
		probeURL := strings.TrimRight(remoteURL, "/") + "/info/refs?service=git-upload-pack"
		client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
		resp, herr := client.Get(probeURL)
		if herr != nil {
			return fmt.Sprintf("error (%v)", herr), true
		}
		resp.Body.Close()
		if resp.StatusCode == 404 {
			return "error (repository not found)", true
		}
		if resp.StatusCode == 401 || resp.StatusCode == 403 {
			return "error (authentication required)", true
		}
	}
	// fetch
	if fout, err := gitCmd(path, "fetch", "origin"); err != nil {
		if strings.Contains(fout, "does not appear to be a git repository") || strings.Contains(fout, "Could not read from remote repository") {
			return "error (repository not found)", true
		}
		if strings.Contains(fout, "couldn't find remote ref") || strings.Contains(fout, "could not find remote ref") {
			return "error (reference not found)", true
		}
		msg := firstLine(fout)
		if msg == "" {
			msg = "failed to fetch"
		}
		return fmt.Sprintf("error (%s)", msg), true
	}
	// Merge FETCH_HEAD (the remote's HEAD / configured upstream as recorded by fetch)
	if _, err := gitCmd(path, "rev-parse", "--verify", "FETCH_HEAD"); err != nil {
		return "error (reference not found)", true
	}
	if !isAncestorOrEqual(path, "HEAD", "FETCH_HEAD") {
		return "error (non-fast-forward update)", true
	}
	if out, err := gitCmd(path, "merge", "--ff-only", "FETCH_HEAD"); err != nil {
		msg := firstLine(out)
		if strings.Contains(out, "Not possible to fast-forward") || strings.Contains(out, "non-fast-forward") || strings.Contains(out, "fatal:") {
			return "error (non-fast-forward update)", true
		}
		if msg == "" {
			msg = "merge failed"
		}
		return fmt.Sprintf("error (%s)", msg), true
	}
	return "ok", false
}

func isAncestorOrEqual(dir, a, b string) bool {
	ah, err1 := gitCmd(dir, "rev-parse", a)
	bh, err2 := gitCmd(dir, "rev-parse", b)
	if err1 != nil || err2 != nil {
		return true // let subsequent logic handle/report
	}
	if ah == bh {
		return true
	}
	_, err := gitCmd(dir, "merge-base", "--is-ancestor", a, b)
	return err == nil
}

func firstLine(s string) string {
	s = strings.TrimSpace(s)
	if idx := strings.Index(s, "\n"); idx >= 0 {
		return strings.TrimSpace(s[:idx])
	}
	return s
}
